content_html:
Brain ⇄ Mind in Memory

In the context of memory and brain functions, what is difference between ‘brain’ and ‘mind’? The brain provides the mechanisms that make memory possible; the mind is the lived experience of memory — coherence, feeling, and meaning.

Brain = physical organ and mechanisms (neurons, synapses, networks).
Mind = emergent subjective experience (awareness, meaning, narrative). Memory sits at their interface: neural plasticity and network dynamics (brain) give rise to recollection and the felt continuity of self (mind).

  • Neural Encoding - Attention, firing patterns, neuromodulators
  • Distributed Storage - Hippocampus↔cortex consolidation
  • Reactivation Dynamics - Theta–gamma coordination
  • Mechanism → Meaning Bridge - Predictive coding, schema, affect tagging. Top‑down goals + bottom‑up salience
  • Experience of Remembering - Vividness, confidence, ownership
  • Narrative & Identity - Coherence, self‑continuity
  • Meaning & Reinterpretation - Context‑dependent reframing

Bidirectional influence: neural dynamics enable experience; experience (attention, goals, reappraisal) modulates neural dynamics over time.

Dimension Brain (Mechanisms) Mind (Experience) Memory Example
Ontology Material: neurons, glia, synapses, oscillations Phenomenal: qualia, awareness, meaning Spiking patterns vs. the felt vividness of a scene
Encoding Attention-modulated firing; hippocampal binding; neuromodulators (ACh, NE) Focus, intention, relevance, emotional significance Attending to a face with strong personal meaning
Storage Systems consolidation; cortical distribution by feature “Knowing”/“Remembering” something belongs to me Semantic facts vs. autobiographical sense of ownership
Recall/Reconstruction Hippocampus ↔ cortex reactivation; theta–gamma coupling Narrative assembly, confidence, nostalgia, self-continuity Recollecting a childhood home with affective tone
Error profile Predictive coding; schema-driven completion Confabulation, bias, suggestion effects Filling in missing details that “fit the story”
Change over time Synaptic plasticity; reconsolidation updates traces Reinterpretation; shifting meaning & identity Same event gains new significance years later
Pathology Lesions, network disconnection, neurotransmitter imbalance Amnesia, depersonalisation, intrusive memories Hippocampal damage → episodic deficits; PTSD flashbacks

References

  • Chalmers, D. J. (1996). The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory. Oxford University Press.
  • Damasio, A. (1999). The Feeling of What Happens: Body and Emotion in the Making of Consciousness. Harcourt.
  • Edelman, G. M., & Tononi, G. (2000). A Universe of Consciousness: How Matter Becomes Imagination. Basic Books.
  • Squire, L. R., & Dede, A. J. (2015). Conscious and unconscious memory systems. Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Biology, 7(3), a021667. https://doi.org/10.1101/cshperspect.a021667
